segments: al-Din Sawab, the chief eunuch of al-Kamil,
sent to Egypt with honor.
And the lord of Hisn Ziyad himself,
with all his household and his wives,
he sent to the sea coast.
And when he had been there for about three years, he secretly put him to death,
and he strongly rebuilt the fortress and the city, and settled them.
And he sent an army again to Samosata,
and laid waste its territory,
but the city itself he was not able to subdue.
Because winter had arrived,
the Sultan left and went to Attalia (or: Adalia,
to Satalia?), a city on the sea coast, to spend the winter in it according to his custom.
And when summer came,
that Sultan gathered troops from various nations, about one hundred thousand horsemen
and a multitude of foot soldiers,
and prepared them to march against the city of Amid.
Then news came to him
that al-Kamil was troubled {OCR?: perturbed} by the treachery committed against him by his son whom he had made king in the South (Yemen).
Therefore the Sultan canceled the expedition against Amid,
because it was very strong
and could only be subdued after a long delay.
And he sent his armies against the city of Edessa in the month of June of the year one thousand five hundred and forty-six
1546 of the Greeks (1235 AD).
And they waged fierce battle against it.
And the Edessenes also fought back very vigorously from within upon the walls.
And in those days, some of the troops of the Romans (Rûm) went against Severek and took it.
And they also went against Callinicus, which is Raqqa,
and they also captured it, and breached it, and plundered it in fury.
Then the people of Harran were afraid,
and they took the keys of Harran and brought them to the Sultan at Melitene.
And he received them,
and sent them back with honor.
The Edessenes, however, were very insolent,
and they even hurled insults at the Sultan.
And because of this the Sultan became enraged,
and he marched against it in person.
Therefore, the armies of the Romans (Rûm) employed every kind of device,
and they subdued it by mines and by ladders which they set up against the walls.
And countless people entered it,
and they took captive and plundered the mansions of the nobles.
And they stripped the men and the women,
and plundered the ornaments of the temples and the holy vessels of the famous churches that were in it.
And they exposed the noble men and noble women,
and brought them out of the city onto the dung-heaps among the tent-curtains,
while they were parched by the intense heat of the days
